summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, professional shampoo and conditioning service: consult with the client, analyse the hair and scalp, choose the right products, shampoo with the correct massage, and condition or treat the hair, including deep treatments with heat. You will also learn to care for natural, textured and chemically treated hair, give aftercare advice, clean up hygienically and keep client records.

blocks.p: This unit covers the whole shampoo and conditioning service, from the moment you greet the client to the moment you clean the basin and fill in her record card. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it is the base for almost every other service you will learn: cutting, styling, colouring, relaxing and braiding all start with hair that has been cleaned and conditioned properly.

A good shampoo relaxes the client and leaves the hair clean, soft and easy to work with. A careless one can scald the scalp, tangle and break the hair, hurt the client's neck or spread an infection to the next client. That is why this unit is about **safety, hygiene and judgement** as much as technique.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practical tasks you shampoo and condition clients with different hair types, including a sectioned shampoo and a deep treatment with heat on natural hair. The assessor watches your consultation, safety, method, clean-up and records, not only the finished hair.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, your hands and the work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Most accidents at the basin are slips, scalds, water or shampoo in the eyes, and strain on the stylist's back or the client's neck. Most infections passed on in salons travel on dirty tools, towels and basins. Good habits prevent both, so learn them before you touch a client.

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Water too hot, or a sudden change in temperature
Scalds; an irritated scalp; faded colour
Test on the inside of your wrist, then ask the client
Keep a finger in the flow and a hand near the tap
If it changes, move the spray away from the head at once
Water or shampoo in the eyes, ears or down the neck
Stinging eyes; discomfort; wet clothes
Cup your hand at the hairline and over the ear
Aim the spray back, away from the face
Seal the gap at the neck with the towel
Water on the floor
Slips and falls
Wipe it up at once
Put out a wet floor sign until it is dry
Electrical equipment near water
Electric shock; fire
Keep dryers, steamers, cables and extension cords away from basins and walkways
Dry your hands before touching plugs and switches
Check cables and plugs; report damage and do not use the item
Leaning back at the basin
Neck pain; dizziness; in rare cases, injury to blood vessels in the neck
Cushion the neck with a neck rest or rolled towel
Do not bend the neck back too far
Help the client sit up slowly
Standing and bending all day
Back strain for you
Stand close to the client, feet apart, back straight
Adjust the chair so you do not stoop or twist
Wet work and products on your hands
Dermatitis (sore, red, cracked or itchy skin)
Wear gloves for products that irritate
Dry your hands well and use hand cream
Report sore skin early

blocks.note: If shampoo gets into the client's eye, rinse the eye gently with plenty of clean, cool water at once, tilting her head so the water runs away from the other eye. Do not let her rub it. If it still stings or looks red, she should get medical help. Record it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (and 220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. Check that a dryer or steamer is made for the socket it is plugged into, and never run a cable across a wet floor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Word
What it means
Example
rows: Cleaning
Removing hair, dirt and product with detergent and water. It always comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt.
Washing a comb in warm, soapy water.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical that kills most harmful germs on tools and surfaces.
Soaking clean combs in disinfectant; wiping the basin with disinfectant.
Contact time
How long a tool or surface must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.
Often several minutes (10 minutes is common), but always the time on the label.
Sterilising
Killing all germs and their spores, usually with an autoclave.
Used for some metal tools in other services.
Antiseptic
A product that reduces germs on the skin.
Hand sanitiser.

blocks.note: A UV cabinet keeps tools that are already clean and disinfected clean while they are stored. It does **not** disinfect dirty tools.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Every client gets clean, disinfected combs, brushes, clips and applicator bottles. A tool that falls on the floor is cleaned and disinfected before it is used again.

To clean a comb or brush: remove the hair, wash it in warm, soapy water, rinse it, put it in disinfectant mixed as the label says for the full contact time, rinse it if the label says, dry it, and store it in a clean, covered container.
Use a fresh towel and gown for every client. Put used ones straight into a **closed laundry bin**, never back on the trolley or chair.
Wash towels and gowns in hot water with detergent (as hot as the fabric allows; 60 °C is a common guide) and dry them completely. Damp towels left in a pile grow bacteria and mildew and soon smell.
Keep clean towels in a closed cupboard, away from dust and spray.
Read the label before you use a product. For chemicals such as disinfectants, read the safety data sheet too.

Keep every product in its own labelled container. Never pour a product into an unlabelled bottle or a food or drink bottle: someone could swallow it or use it wrongly, and the directions and warnings are lost.
Use pumps, or a clean spatula for tubs. Do not put your fingers into a tub, because that puts germs into the product.
Put lids back on, wipe drips off the bottles, and store them upright.
Store products in a cool, dry place out of direct sunlight, away from water heaters and dryers. Jamaica's heat can make products separate, spoil or lose strength, and aerosols can burst.
Use the oldest stock first (first in, first out). Check expiry dates and the open-jar symbol: '12M' means use within 12 months of opening.

Mix disinfectants exactly as the label says. Too weak will not kill the germs; too strong can harm skin, tools and surfaces. Never mix two cleaning chemicals together: some, such as bleach and ammonia cleaners, give off a poisonous gas.
Report leaking, damaged or low stock to your supervisor.

blocks.p: You cannot choose the right products or method unless you understand what you are cleaning. This section covers how a hair is built, where its natural oil comes from, and the hair characteristics you check at every consultation.
Each hair grows from a **follicle**, a small pocket in the skin of the scalp. The part above the skin is the **hair shaft**. It has three layers.

head: Layer
What it is
Why it matters in this unit
rows: Cuticle
The outer layer: thin, clear, overlapping scales, like tiles on a roof, with their free edges pointing towards the ends.
Flat, smooth cuticle: the hair shines, holds moisture and tangles less
Raised or damaged cuticle: the hair feels rough, looks dull, tangles, and loses moisture and colour
Alkaline products and heat lift it; acid-balanced products and a cool rinse help it lie flat
Cortex
The middle layer and the bulk of the hair: long fibres of keratin (a protein) held together by bonds. It holds the natural colour and much of the hair's moisture.
Gives the hair its strength and stretch (elasticity)
Relaxers and permanent colour work here
Deep (penetrating) treatments aim to reach it
Medulla
The soft centre of the hair. It may be missing in fine hair.
It makes little difference to shampooing and conditioning.

ul: **Sebaceous glands** open into each hair follicle and make **sebum**, the natural oil that keeps the scalp and hair soft and protected.

On straight hair, sebum travels easily down the strand, so straight hair looks oily sooner. On curly and coily hair, sebum cannot travel easily round the bends, so the lengths are often dry even when the scalp is oily.
Sweat, dead skin cells, dust and styling products mix with the sebum on the scalp. Shampooing removes this mix.
A healthy scalp is clean and free of redness, sores and heavy flaking. Healthy skin and hair are slightly acid (about pH 4.5 to 5.5), and this 'acid mantle' helps protect the skin from germs.

head: Characteristic
What it means
How to check
What it tells you
rows: Texture
The thickness of one single hair: **fine**, **medium** or **coarse**.
Feel a single hair between your finger and thumb, and compare it with hairs you know.
Fine hair is easily weighed down, so use light products. Coarse hair may take longer to wet and to take in products.
Density
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp: **low** (thin), **medium** or **high** (thick).
Move the hair aside in a few places and see how much scalp shows.
High-density hair needs more product, more time and sections, so that water and shampoo reach the scalp.
Porosity
How easily the hair takes in and loses water. It depends on the state of the cuticle.
Hold a small dry strand by the ends and slide the finger and thumb of your other hand along it towards the scalp. Also watch how fast the hair soaks up water.
Smooth: low porosity (tight cuticle)
Slightly rough: normal to porous
Very rough, soaks up water at once: high porosity
Elasticity
How far the hair stretches and then returns to its length without breaking.
Take a single wet hair, hold both ends and stretch it gently.
Stretches and springs back: good
Snaps after very little stretch: poor, usually dry; needs moisture
Stretches a long way, does not spring back, feels gummy: weak; needs protein
Curl pattern
Straight, wavy, curly or coily (tightly coiled).
Look at clean hair with no product in it.
The tighter the curl, the more the hair tangles, shrinks and dries out, and the more gently it must be handled.
Condition
How healthy the hair is: normal, dry, oily, damaged or chemically treated.
Look, feel, and ask about her hair's history.
Guides your choice of shampoo, conditioner and treatment.

blocks.h: Porosity and what to do about it

head: Porosity
Signs
What to do
rows: Low
Smooth; water beads on the hair; slow to wet and slow to dry; products seem to sit on top.
Use light products; apply them to wet, warm hair; gentle heat helps a deep treatment go in.
Normal
Takes in water at a steady rate; looks healthy and shiny.
Keep it that way: a suitable shampoo, regular conditioner and gentle handling.
High
Rough; soaks up water at once and dries fast; tangles; often dull, frizzy, or chemically treated.
Condition every wash and give treatments as the hair needs; use acid-balanced products and a cool final rinse; handle gently.

blocks.note: **Texture and density are not the same.** A client who says her hair is 'thick' may have a great many fine hairs: fine texture, high density. Check and record both.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: As a guide, healthy wet hair can stretch by up to about half its length and spring back; dry hair stretches much less. The 'float test' (dropping a hair into a glass of water), popular online, is not reliable, because oils and products on the hair change how it floats. Use the slide test and watch how the hair takes up water.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The consultation is a short, private conversation before the service. You find out what the client wants, check that her hair and scalp are fit for the service, agree a plan and record it. Do it at the styling chair, with the hair dry and in good light, before she goes to the basin.

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask your questions
Look at and feel the hair and scalp
Test porosity and elasticity
Check for contra-indications
Explain your plan, products and price
Agree and record

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants today, and how she will wear her hair
Lets you plan the products, the finish and the services that follow.
When she last washed her hair, and what she uses at home (gels, edge control, grease, oils, sprays)
Tells you about build-up, helps you choose a clarifying or a gentle shampoo, and shapes your aftercare advice.
Chemical services (relaxer, texturiser, colour, bleach, perm, smoothing treatment), and when
Treated hair needs gentle products. Some chemical services need an unwashed scalp, and the scalp must not be scratched before one.
Allergies, sensitive skin, or any past reaction to a product
So you can avoid ingredients that could cause a reaction. Read the labels.
Scalp problems: itching, soreness, flaking
Points you to conditions you must look for.
Health and comfort: neck or back problems, recent surgery, dizziness, pregnancy
She may need a front-wash basin, extra support or a shorter time at the basin, or the service may need to wait.
The next service (cut, colour, relaxer, braids)
The shampoo and conditioner must suit what comes next. Follow that product's instructions.

ul: Part the hair in several places across the head, under good light.
Look closely at the hairline, the **nape** (the back of the neck, where the hairline ends) and behind the ears, where many problems show first.
Feel gently with the pads of your fingers, never your nails.
Look for flakes, redness, sores, cuts, scabs, swelling, bald or broken patches, and anything moving on the scalp or stuck to the hairs.

blocks.p: A **contra-indication** is anything that means the service should not go ahead, or must be changed. A **contagious** (infectious) condition, one that can pass from person to person, stops the service. Other contra-indications mean you adapt: a client who cannot lean back is washed at a front-wash basin or sitting up; a sensitive scalp gets mild products and light massage; a client with an allergy gets products without that ingredient.

head: Condition
What you see
Contagious?
What you do
rows: Dandruff (pityriasis capitis)
Small white or grey dry flakes that brush off easily; the scalp may itch. No redness or sores.
No
Carry on. Use an anti-dandruff (medicated) shampoo and advise on home care.
Dry scalp
Fine, dry flakes and a tight feeling; no redness.
No
Carry on with moisturising products and water that is not too hot.
Oily scalp (seborrhoea)
Greasy shine on the scalp; hair goes lank soon after washing.
No
Carry on. Shampoo for oily hair, warm (not hot) water, lighter massage, conditioner on the ends only.
Psoriasis or eczema
Psoriasis: thick, silvery scales on red, raised patches. Eczema: red, dry, itchy skin that may crack or weep.
No
If the skin is unbroken, work gently with mild products. If it is broken, bleeding or very inflamed, do not shampoo; suggest she sees a doctor.
Head lice (pediculosis capitis)
Small grey-brown insects; tiny oval eggs (**nits**) glued to the hairs close to the scalp, mostly at the nape and behind the ears; itching.
Yes
Do not carry out the service. Tell the client (or parent) in private and suggest a pharmacist or doctor.
Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis)
Round, scaly patches; broken hairs or bald patches; sometimes red rings or swelling. A fungal infection.
Yes
Do not carry out the service. Refer her to a doctor.
Impetigo
Sores or blisters that weep and form honey-coloured crusts. A bacterial infection.
Yes
Do not carry out the service. Refer her to a doctor.
Boils or infected follicles (folliculitis)
Red, painful lumps or pus spots around the hairs.
Can spread
Do not work over them. Refer her to a doctor.
Cuts, grazes, sores or recent stitches
Broken skin.
No, but germs can get in
Do not shampoo over broken skin: shampoo stings and germs can enter. Postpone, or refer her if it looks infected.
Traction alopecia
Thinning or bald patches at the hairline or edges, from styles that pull too tightly.
No
Carry on gently, with no pulling. Advise looser styles; suggest a doctor if it is severe.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not tell the client she has a disease, and never try to treat an infection or infestation yourself. Describe what you have seen, quietly and in private, explain why the service cannot go ahead today, and advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist. Write it on the record card.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: After a client with a contagious condition: bag her towels and gown for a hot wash, clean and then disinfect every tool and surface she touched (combs, clips, chair, neck rest, basin), and wash your hands.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Head lice spread easily among children who play and sit close together, and they are no sign of a dirty home. Speak to the parent kindly and privately, never in front of other clients or the child's friends.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The **pH scale** shows how acid or alkaline a product is. It runs from 0 to 14. **7 is neutral** (pure water). Below 7 is **acid**; above 7 is **alkaline**. Each step on the scale is a change of ten times, so pH 9 is a hundred times more alkaline than pH 7, and pH 4 is ten times more acid than pH 5.

head: pH
Examples
Effect on the hair
rows: About 2 to 3 (strong acid)
Lemon juice, vinegar
Too strong to use undiluted on the hair.
About 3.5 to 6 (mild acid)
Most conditioners; acid-balanced shampoos (about 4.5 to 5.5)
Smooths and tightens the cuticle; adds shine; helps hold moisture and colour in.
7 (neutral)
Pure water
The hair takes in water and swells a little.
About 8 to 11 (alkaline)
Soap, some strong cleansers, permanent colour
Swells the hair and lifts the cuticle; the hair can feel rough and tangle.
About 12 to 14 (strong alkali)
Most relaxers
Breaks bonds inside the hair and can burn the skin. Relaxing is taught in its own unit.

blocks.p: Healthy hair and skin are about pH 4.5 to 5.5. That is why **acid-balanced** shampoos and conditioners are gentle: they work close to the hair's own pH and help keep the cuticle smooth and flat. After an alkaline service such as colour or a relaxer, acid-balanced products help bring the hair back to its normal pH.

Oil and water do not mix, so water alone cannot wash sebum, oils and styling products out of the hair. Shampoo contains **surfactants** (surface active agents), also called **detergents**. Each surfactant molecule has two ends: a **head** that is attracted to water and a **tail** that is attracted to oil.

flow: The tails attach to oil and dirt on the hair and scalp
Massage loosens the oil and breaks it into small droplets
The surfactant surrounds each droplet, heads facing out
The heads hold the droplets in the water
The rinse water carries them away

ul: The main job of a shampoo is to **lift dirt, oil and product build-up off the hair and scalp** without harming them. Surfactants also help water spread over and soak into the hair.

**Lather** (the foam) comes from surfactants and air. Lots of lather does not mean better cleaning. Oil, dirt and hard water all cut down lather, which is why a first shampoo on oily hair often lathers poorly and a second one lathers well.

Strong surfactants called **sulphates** (for example sodium lauryl sulphate) clean very well but can strip moisture and fade colour. **Sulphate-free** shampoos use milder surfactants and lather less; they suit dry, natural, relaxed and coloured hair.

blocks.note: In many parts of Jamaica the water comes from limestone rock and is **hard**: it carries dissolved minerals such as calcium and magnesium. Hard water makes shampoo lather poorly and can leave a dull film on the hair. A **chelating** shampoo (a clarifying shampoo made to remove minerals) lifts the film; always follow it with conditioner.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Shampooing, combing, heat, sun, sea water and chemicals all roughen the cuticle. Damaged hair carries a small negative electrical charge. Most conditioners contain positively charged ingredients that are drawn to the damaged areas and cling there. This **smooths the cuticle**, cuts static and tangles, and makes the hair easier to comb. Most conditioners are also slightly acid, which helps the cuticle lie flat.

head: Ingredient type
What it does
rows: Conditioning agents (positively charged)
Cling to damaged areas; smooth the cuticle; reduce static and tangles.
Oils, butters and silicones
Coat the hair; add shine and slip; slow down moisture loss. Some build up if they are never washed out.
Humectants (for example glycerin)
Draw water in and help the hair hold it.
Proteins (hydrolysed, meaning broken into small pieces)
Fill gaps in weak or damaged hair and strengthen it for a time.

blocks.note: Conditioner smooths and protects the hair, but it cannot mend it for good. Split ends cannot be joined back together: the only cure is to cut them off.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Shampoo
Use it for
Take care
rows: Everyday (normal)
Normal hair and scalp.
Choose a milder type if the hair is dry or treated.
Moisturising
Dry hair; natural, curly and coily hair; relaxed hair.
Can weigh down fine or oily hair.
Clarifying (deep-cleansing)
Heavy build-up of gels, edge control, oils, butters and sprays; before some services when the maker says.
Strong: not for every wash. It can dry the hair and fade colour, so always condition afterwards.
Chelating
A mineral film from hard water; chlorine from swimming pools.
As for clarifying. Condition afterwards.
Anti-dandruff (medicated)
Dandruff and a flaky, itchy scalp.
Leave it on the scalp for the time on the label. It does not treat infections: refer those.
Colour-care
Coloured hair.
Mild, usually sulphate-free and acid-balanced, to slow fading.
Sulphate-free
Coloured, relaxed, lightened, dry and natural hair.
Lathers less: this is normal.
For oily hair
An oily scalp.
Still choose a gentle one, and use warm, not hot, water.
Volumising
Fine, limp hair.
Can be drying on coarse or dry hair.
Neutralising (for relaxers)
Only at the end of a relaxer service, to stop the relaxer and bring the hair back to its normal acid pH. Many change colour if relaxer is still in the hair.
Not for ordinary shampoos. You will use it in the relaxing unit.
Co-wash (cleansing conditioner)
Washing dry, curly and coily hair gently between shampoos.
Does not remove heavy build-up; use a shampoo or clarifier now and then.
Dry shampoo
Soaking up oil between washes (powder or spray).
Not a real wash; it builds up on the scalp if overused.

head: Type
What it does
When to use it
Time and heat
rows: Rinse-out (surface or instant) conditioner
Coats and smooths the cuticle; detangles; cuts static; adds shine. Works on the outside of the hair.
After most shampoos.
Usually 1 to 5 minutes, no heat; then rinse. Follow the label.
Leave-in conditioner
A light conditioner that stays in the hair: moisture, slip for detangling, some protection from heat and sun.
After the final rinse, before styling; dry, curly, coily and chemically treated hair.
Not rinsed out.
Deep (penetrating) conditioner or treatment
A richer product whose small molecules pass through a lifted cuticle into the cortex.
Dry, porous, damaged or chemically treated hair; often every 1 to 4 weeks, as the hair needs.
Often 10 to 30 minutes, usually with heat. Follow the maker.
Protein treatment
Puts protein into weak hair and strengthens it for a time.
Weak, limp, over-stretchy or gummy hair; after chemical damage.
Only now and then, as the maker says. Too much leaves the hair hard and brittle.
Moisturising treatment
Puts back water and softness with humectants and oils.
Dry, hard, brittle hair that snaps easily.
Regularly, as the hair needs; heat helps it work.
Hot oil treatment
Warm oil softens dry hair and a dry scalp.
Dry hair and scalp.
Warm, not hot: test it on your wrist first.
Scalp treatment
A product made for a dry, oily or flaky scalp.
When the scalp needs care.
As the label says.

head: Client
Shampoo
Conditioner
rows: Fine, straight hair; oily scalp
Shampoo for oily hair (two washes if needed)
A light rinse-out on the mid-lengths and ends only.
Dry, coily natural hair
Moisturising, sulphate-free shampoo or a co-wash, in sections
A rich rinse-out or a deep moisturising treatment, then a leave-in.
Relaxed hair
A mild, moisturising shampoo
Moisture at every wash; protein now and then; a leave-in.
Coloured or lightened hair
Colour-care, sulphate-free, acid-balanced
Colour-care conditioner; protein and moisture for lightened hair.
Heavy product build-up
Clarifying shampoo (two washes if needed)
A conditioner afterwards to put back softness.
Dandruff
Anti-dandruff shampoo, left on for the label's time
A light conditioner on the lengths, not the scalp.
Hard-water film or swimmer's hair
Chelating shampoo
A moisturising conditioner.

blocks.note: Read every label before you use a product, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for amount, time and heat. If the label and your habit disagree, the label wins; if you are unsure, ask your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: At the basin: preparing and shampooing

ul: Basin, taps, spray hose, neck rest and chair cleaned and disinfected; drain clear of hair.
Clean towels, gown and cape ready; wide-tooth comb, clips and the chosen products within reach (not on the floor).
Hot and cold water both working; spray hose and pressure checked.
Floor dry; dryers and steamers set up away from the basin.
Your hands washed, nails short and smooth; rings, bracelets and watches that could scratch taken off.

blocks.note: Water lock-offs happen, especially in dry spells. Before you start a shampoo, check there is enough water, and know where the salon's tank and pump switch are. Never start a service you cannot rinse out. If the salon uses a solar water heater, the water can be very hot on a sunny afternoon: test it every time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Ask her to remove earrings, necklaces and glasses and keep them safe
Tuck in her collar
Put on a clean gown
Place a clean towel around her shoulders
Add a waterproof cape if your salon uses one
Check it is secure but not tight at the neck

ul: **Back-wash basin** (the most common): the client sits well back in the chair. Support her head with your hand as you lower it gently into the basin, with a neck rest or rolled towel cushioning her neck. The towel and gown should seal the gap so that water runs into the basin, not down her back.
Ask: 'Is your neck comfortable? Is the chair all right?' Adjust the chair until it is.
**Front-wash basin**: the client leans forward over the basin and holds a towel or face cloth over her eyes. Use it for clients who cannot lean back, such as those with neck problems.
Keep the time with her head back as short as the work allows, and watch for signs of discomfort.

blocks.note: Bending the neck back hard over the edge of a basin for a long time can, in rare cases, injure blood vessels in the neck and cause dizziness or even a stroke, especially in older clients. Always cushion the neck and do not over-stretch it. Stop at once if the client feels dizzy, sick, numb or unwell, and get help.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Run the water and test it on the **inside of your wrist**, which is sensitive like the scalp. Then ask the client as soon as it touches her head, and check with her again during the service.

Most clients like **warm** water, about body temperature; the client's comfort decides. Water that is too hot can scald, irritate the scalp, dry the hair and fade colour. Water that is too cold is uncomfortable and does not lift oil well.
Keep part of your hand in the flow so you feel any change first, and keep a hand near the tap. The temperature can jump when someone turns on another tap or when a tank or heater runs low.
Check the pressure. Too strong is uncomfortable, splashes and tangles long or fragile hair; too weak rinses poorly and slows the service.
Hold the spray close to the scalp, aimed back towards the basin and away from the face. Cup your hand at the hairline and over the ear.
Remove pins, clips and bands, and check for clip-in extensions.

Gently brush or finger-detangle to loosen tangles and loose hairs. Do **not** brush before a chemical service, because brushing can scratch the scalp. Finger-detangle natural, coily hair in sections (see 'Natural, textured and chemically treated hair').
Apply a pre-shampoo treatment (pre-poo) if you planned one.

flow: Seat the client, support her neck and check she is comfortable
Test the water on your wrist, then ask the client
Wet the hair right through to the scalp, cupping your hand at the hairline; lift the head gently to wet the nape
Put shampoo in your palm, spread it over both hands and apply it evenly over the scalp
Massage with the finger pads in a set pattern: front hairline, over the top to the nape, then the sides and behind the ears
Squeeze the lather down the lengths; do not pile the hair up or rub it
Rinse until the water runs clear and no lather or slippery feel is left
Shampoo a second time if needed
Squeeze out the extra water before you condition

blocks.p: Working in a **set pattern** makes sure the whole scalp is cleaned and nothing is missed, and it feels calm and professional to the client.

ul: **How much shampoo?** Enough to suit the length and density of the hair. Start with a small amount (about a teaspoon for short hair) and add more if you need it. Too much wastes product and is hard to rinse out; too little does not clean.

**Why a second shampoo?** The first lifts most of the oil and dirt and often lathers poorly. On very dirty or oily hair, or hair with build-up, a second shampoo finishes the cleaning and lathers well. A medicated shampoo is often used for the second wash and left on for the label's time.
**Long hair:** let the lengths hang down into the basin and squeeze the lather through them. Piling long hair on top of the head and rubbing it causes tangles, especially in curly and coily hair.

blocks.p: Scalp massage loosens dirt, oil and dead skin, increases the blood flow to the scalp, spreads the product evenly and relaxes the client. Always use the **pads of your fingers**, never the nails.

head: Movement
How you do it
When you use it
rows: Effleurage
Light, slow, smooth stroking with the palms or the flat of the fingers, with an even pressure.
To start and finish the massage; to spread shampoo or conditioner; during conditioning. It soothes and relaxes.
Rotary
Small, firm circles with the finger pads, moving the hands over the head in a set pattern.
The main shampoo movement: it loosens dirt and oil and builds the lather.
Friction
Quick, brisk rubbing with the finger pads, in short bursts.
During the shampoo, after rotary, to stimulate the scalp and help lift dirt and dead skin. Leave it out on a tender scalp and before a chemical service.
Petrissage
Slow, firm kneading: the finger pads press and lift the scalp, moving it over the bone beneath.
During conditioning treatments and scalp massage (not usually in a basic shampoo). It relaxes the client and helps the treatment work in.

blocks.note: Nails scratch the scalp. Scratches sting, let germs in, and let chemicals burn the scalp if a chemical service follows.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: When to keep the massage light, or leave it out

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A chemical service comes next (relaxer, colour, perm)
Light movements only: no friction, no scratching, no brushing first. Most relaxers must go on an unwashed scalp, so check the maker's instructions before you shampoo at all.
Tender, sensitive or inflamed scalp; psoriasis or eczema
Very light pressure and mild products; avoid any broken skin.
Cuts, grazes or recent surgery
No massage over the area; you may not be able to shampoo at all.
Oily scalp
Keep the movements lighter and the water warm, not hot. Firm, stimulating massage and hot water can make the scalp produce more oil.
Fragile or thinning hair; traction alopecia at the edges
Gentle pressure; do not tug the hair.
Braids, locs, weaves and extensions
Press and pat; do not rub (see 'Natural, textured and chemically treated hair').
The client asks for less pressure, or has a headache or neck pain
Do as she asks. Her comfort comes first.

ul: Rinse until the water runs clear and the hair no longer feels slippery. Check the **nape**, behind the ears and along the hairline, where shampoo and conditioner are easily left behind.
Shampoo left in the hair dulls it, can irritate the scalp, leaves flakes that look like dandruff, and can affect the next service.

Remove water by **squeezing** the hair and **blotting** it with a clean towel. Do not rub: wet hair is weaker and stretches easily, and rubbing roughens the cuticle, causing frizz, tangles and breakage.

flow: Squeeze the extra water out of the hair
Put the conditioner in your palm and spread it over both hands
Apply it mainly to the mid-lengths and ends
Spread it with effleurage, or comb it through with a wide-tooth comb, starting at the ends
Leave it for the time on the label
Rinse thoroughly, finishing with cool or lukewarm water

ul: **Why the mid-lengths and ends?** They are the oldest, driest part of the hair. The roots get sebum from the scalp, and conditioner on the roots can make fine or oily hair limp.
**Why squeeze out the water first?** Extra water dilutes the conditioner and stops it reaching the hair.

**Why comb from the ends?** Combing from the roots pushes small knots down into one big tangle, which then tears the hair. Start at the ends and work up a little at a time, with a wide-tooth comb or your fingers.
**Why a cool final rinse?** It helps the cuticle lie flat, which adds shine and helps hold moisture in. Keep it comfortable for the client.

blocks.p: Hair needs a balance of protein (strength) and moisture (softness and stretch). Use the elasticity and porosity tests, and how the hair feels, to decide.

head: What you find
What it usually means
What to choose
rows: Hard, rough, dry or straw-like; snaps after very little stretch
Lacking moisture
A moisturising (deep) treatment
Soft, limp, mushy or gummy when wet; stretches a long way and does not spring back
Weak: lacking protein
A protein treatment, followed by moisture
Stiff and brittle after many protein treatments
Too much protein
Stop protein for now; use moisturising treatments
Healthy feel; good stretch and return
Balanced
Keep it up with regular conditioning

blocks.note: The balance changes from visit to visit, especially after colour, relaxers, heat styling or a lot of sea and sun. Test the hair every time; do not just repeat the last treatment.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Giving a deep conditioning treatment with heat

flow: Consult, test porosity and elasticity, and choose a protein or moisturising treatment
Shampoo the hair, so the treatment can reach clean hair
Squeeze and blot out the extra water
Divide the hair into sections
Apply the treatment section by section, from the mid-lengths to the ends (and to the roots only if the maker says)
Comb it through gently from the ends with a wide-tooth comb or your fingers
Cover the hair with a plastic processing cap
Put the client under the heat the maker says (hood dryer, steamer or heat cap) and start a timer
Check on her every few minutes
When the time is up, let the hair cool briefly if the maker says, then rinse thoroughly with lukewarm water and finish cool

ul: Gentle heat lifts the cuticle a little and speeds up the product, so more of it gets into the hair.
The **plastic cap** holds in warmth and moisture, stops the treatment drying out on the hair, and keeps the client clean.
Too much heat, or too long, can make the client uncomfortable, irritate or burn the scalp, and dry out the hair. A protein treatment left on too long can leave the hair hard and brittle.
Not every treatment uses heat. Read the label.

head: Equipment
Type of heat
Check before and after use
rows: Hood dryer
Dry heat
Clean; cable and plug undamaged
Set to the heat the maker says (usually low to medium)
Hood lowered over the cap; client comfortable
Steamer
Moist heat (steam)
Water tank filled with the water the maker says (many say distilled water, as hard water leaves scale)
Warmed up before the client sits under it
Check the hood and water level: hot drips can scald
Emptied, cleaned and descaled as the maker says
Heat cap (thermal cap)
Dry heat from a heated cap worn over the plastic cap
Cap and cable undamaged
Heat set as the maker says

blocks.note: Write down the time or set a timer the moment the client goes under the heat. Example: the treatment goes on at 2:40 p.m. and the maker says 15 minutes, so you rinse at 2:55 p.m. Most deep treatments take about 10 to 30 minutes, but always use the time on the product, not a guess.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Never leave a client under a dryer or steamer and forget her. Check every few minutes and ask if she is comfortable. Switch off and move the equipment away at once if she feels too hot, faint or unwell. Keep cables tidy and away from water.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: After the final rinse, blot the hair and apply a leave-in conditioner through the lengths, especially on dry, curly, coily and chemically treated hair. It adds moisture and slip for detangling, and gives some protection during styling. Many natural-hair clients then seal the moisture in with a light oil or cream.

sections.title: Natural, textured and chemically treated hair

blocks.h: Why coily hair needs extra care

ul: Every bend in a coil is a weak point where the hair can break.
Sebum cannot travel easily down a coil, so the lengths are dry even when the scalp is oily.
Coils wrap around each other, making tangles and single-strand knots. Wet hair shrinks, so it tangles even more.
Coily hair breaks easily when it is dry or handled roughly. Gentle hands and plenty of moisture prevent most damage.

blocks.h: Sectioned shampoo for long or dense natural hair

flow: Apply a pre-poo (oil or conditioner on the dry lengths) if planned
Finger-detangle gently, working from the ends up
Divide the hair into 4 to 8 sections and twist or clip each one
Wet the hair thoroughly, making sure the water reaches the scalp
Shampoo the scalp one section at a time with the finger pads; squeeze the lather down the lengths
Rinse each section and twist it up again
Condition each section and detangle it with your fingers, then a wide-tooth comb, from the ends to the roots
Rinse, finishing cool
Blot with a microfibre towel or a soft cotton T-shirt
Apply a leave-in and put the hair in large twists or plaits, with snag-free bands, to keep it stretched

head: Practice
What it is
Why it helps
rows: Pre-poo
Oil or conditioner put on the dry hair before the shampoo.
Protects the lengths from being stripped and makes detangling easier.
Co-washing
Washing with a cleansing conditioner instead of shampoo, between shampoos.
Cleans gently without stripping moisture. A shampoo or clarifier is still needed now and then to remove build-up.
Low manipulation
Handling the hair as little as possible: fewer combings, gentle detangling, protective styles.
Less breakage, so the hair keeps its length.
Stretching
Large twists, plaits, banding or threading after washing.
Stops the hair shrinking and tangling as it dries.
Sealing
A light oil or butter over the leave-in.
Slows down moisture loss.
Night protection
A satin or silk bonnet, scarf or pillowcase.
Cotton soaks up moisture and rubs the hair; satin does not.

blocks.note: Never pile coily hair on top of the head and scrub it. Keep each section apart, squeeze the lather through, and let the water run down the lengths.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Mix shampoo with water in an **applicator bottle** and put it on the scalp along the parts.
Press and pat the scalp with the finger pads. Do not rub or scrub the braids: it causes frizz, loosens them and lifts the roots.
Squeeze the lather down the braids and rinse very well. Shampoo left behind causes itching and flakes.
Use a light, diluted conditioner or a leave-in spray; heavy creams build up.
Squeeze out the water, blot, and **dry fully**, under a hood dryer if needed. Braids and weaves that stay damp can smell of mildew.
For sew-in weaves, clean the scalp between the tracks with the applicator bottle and make sure the hair under the weave dries completely.
Check for bumps, soreness or thinning at the hairline: signs that the style is too tight (traction alopecia).
Use a **residue-free** (clarifying) shampoo that rinses out cleanly. Creamy shampoos, heavy conditioners, waxes and butters get trapped inside locs and build up.
Apply the shampoo to the scalp and **squeeze** it through each loc like a sponge. Do not rub.
Rinse very thoroughly, then squeeze out as much water as you can.
**Dry the locs right through.** Thick locs can stay wet inside for hours, and damp locs can grow mildew and smell musty.
Young (starter) locs unravel easily: wash them gently, with as little handling as possible.

blocks.note: Many clients wear locs for religious or cultural reasons, for example as members of the Rastafari faith. Ask how they want their locs handled and which products they will accept, and respect their wishes.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A relaxer straightens the hair for good by breaking bonds in the cortex. Relaxed hair is weaker and more porous than natural hair, and it loses moisture easily.

The **line of demarcation**, where the new growth meets the relaxed hair, is the weakest point. Detangle from the ends, and hold the hair firmly between that line and the scalp so that combing does not pull on it.
Use mild, moisturising (often sulphate-free) shampoos; condition at every wash; give protein and moisture treatments as the hair needs; do not clarify too often.
Before a relaxer, follow the relaxer maker's instructions: most must go on an unwashed scalp, and the scalp must not be scratched. Neutralising shampoo is used only during the relaxer service.
Colour fades when the cuticle is lifted: strong or clarifying shampoos, very hot water, sun, sea water and chlorine all speed it up.
Use colour-care, sulphate-free, acid-balanced products, lukewarm water and a cool final rinse.
Follow the colour maker's advice on how soon after colouring the hair may be shampooed.
Lightened (bleached) hair is very porous and fragile: balance protein and moisture, detangle with great care and keep heat low.
After a smoothing (keratin-type) treatment, use the shampoo that treatment's maker recommends, usually sulphate-free.

blocks.note: Sun, sea and swimming pools are part of life here, and they dry the hair and fade colour. Advise clients to wet the hair with fresh water and apply a leave-in before swimming, rinse with fresh water straight after, and cover the hair in strong sun.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Give a final rinse and check the nape, behind the ears and the hairline
Squeeze out the water
Wrap the hair in a clean towel
Support her head and help her sit up slowly; ask how she feels
Blot the hair; dry her face, ears and neck if needed
Detangle from the ends with a wide-tooth comb or fingers
Apply a leave-in or other products as planned
Take her to the styling area

blocks.note: Some clients feel light-headed when they sit up after lying back. Let her sit for a moment before she stands, and stay with her until she feels steady.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Aftercare tells the client how to keep her hair healthy until her next visit. Base it on what you found in the consultation, give the reason for each point, and keep it simple.

head: Client
Advice
Why
rows: Dry or damaged hair
Gentle, moisturising shampoo; do not wash more often than needed
Conditioner every wash; a deep treatment about every 1 to 2 weeks, as the product says
Leave-in conditioner; less heat, and a heat protectant
Wide-tooth comb from the ends; satin bonnet or pillowcase at night
Puts moisture back and stops further breakage.
Oily scalp
Shampoo for oily hair as often as she needs
Warm, not hot, water; no hard scrubbing
Conditioner on the ends only
No heavy grease or oils on the scalp
Controls oil without irritating the scalp or causing build-up.
Natural, coily hair
Wash in sections; co-wash between shampoos
Detangle with conditioner, from the ends
Low-manipulation and protective styles
Satin or silk at night
Keeps moisture in and cuts breakage.
Relaxed hair
Mild, moisturising shampoo; keep protein and moisture in balance
Be gentle at the new growth
Relaxer touch-ups on the new growth only, when her stylist advises
Relaxed hair is weaker, and the line where new growth meets relaxed hair breaks easily.
Coloured hair
Colour-care, sulphate-free shampoo and conditioner
Lukewarm water; cool final rinse
Protect the hair from sun, sea and chlorine
Slows fading and keeps the cuticle smooth.
Braids and locs
Wash the scalp with diluted shampoo; dry fully
Light products; no heavy creams or waxes
Do not keep braids in too long (many stylists advise about 6 to 8 weeks)
Prevents build-up, mildew and damage from tension.
Dandruff
Anti-dandruff shampoo, left on for the time on the label
See a doctor if it does not improve, or if the scalp is red or sore
Controls flaking; anything more needs medical advice.

ul: Recommend products that suit her hair, usually the ones you used today, and explain why they suit her.
Tell her how to use them: how much, how often, and on which part of the hair.
Be honest and do not pressure her: she decides. Know the prices in JMD.
Suggest when she should come back, for example for her next treatment, and book it if she wants.
Record what she buys on her record card.

blocks.note: Good product advice is part of the service, not a sales trick. If a client goes home and uses a harsh product, the good work you did today is soon undone.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Put on gloves and remove the hair from the basin and drain trap; bin it
Clean the basin, taps, spray hose, neck rest and chair with detergent and water
Wipe them with disinfectant and leave it for the contact time
Put used towels and gowns in the closed laundry bin
Clean and disinfect the combs, brushes and clips
Put lids back on products, wipe the bottles and return them to their place
Dry the floor; leave a wet floor sign out until it is dry
Wash and dry your hands

blocks.p: At the end of the day: launder the towels and gowns and dry them completely; empty, clean and dry the steamer as the maker says; wipe down the dryers; restock the basin area; and report faulty equipment and low stock.

Write on the client's **record card** (or the salon's computer record) at every visit. It lets the next stylist choose products safely, shows what worked, and is evidence of what was done if there is a complaint or a reaction.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's name and contact details
07/11/2026, Shanique Brown, Portmore
Hair analysis
Natural, coily; fine texture, high density; high porosity; poor elasticity (snaps)
Scalp
Clean, slightly dry; no contra-indications seen
Products used
Moisturising sulphate-free shampoo (2 washes); moisturising deep treatment; leave-in conditioner
Heat and timing
Steamer, 20 minutes, as the maker's instructions say
Reactions or problems
None
Advice given
Co-wash weekly; deep treatment every 2 weeks; satin bonnet at night
Products bought
Leave-in conditioner, JMD 2,200
Stylist
T. Morgan (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure: store cards in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, let only staff who need them see them, and never discuss a client's hair or scalp with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can name the hazards at the basin and say how to prevent scalds, slips, shocks, eye accidents, neck strain and back strain.
I can explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and why a UV cabinet does not disinfect.
I can launder towels correctly and handle and store products safely.
I can describe the cuticle, cortex and medulla, and say where sebum comes from.
I can check and record hair texture, density, porosity, elasticity and condition.
I can carry out a consultation and say why each question matters.
I can recognise dandruff, oily and dry scalp, psoriasis, head lice, ringworm and impetigo, and say which are contagious.
I can explain why a contagious condition stops the service and how to refer the client tactfully.
I can explain the pH scale and why acid-balanced products are gentle on the hair.
I can explain how surfactants in shampoo lift oil and dirt.
I can choose shampoos and conditioners for oily, dry, natural, relaxed, coloured and dandruff-prone hair, and for build-up and hard water.
I can gown a client, seat her safely at a back-wash or front-wash basin, and test and control the water.
I can shampoo in a set pattern with effleurage, rotary and friction, using my finger pads, and say when to keep massage light.
I can apply rinse-out and leave-in conditioners and detangle from the ends.
I can choose a protein or moisturising treatment from the elasticity and porosity tests.
I can give a deep treatment with a cap and heat, timed as the maker says, checking the client throughout.
I can shampoo natural hair in sections, and wash braids and locs without damaging them.
I can care for relaxed, coloured and lightened hair with gentle products.
I can finish the service, give aftercare and product advice, clean up the basin and tools, and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I test the water on my wrist and ask the client, so that she is not scalded.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The outer layer of the hair: overlapping scales that lie flat when the hair is healthy.
The middle layer of the hair, made of keratin; gives strength and elasticity and holds colour.
Glands attached to the hair follicles that make sebum.
The thickness of a single hair: fine, medium or coarse.
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp.
How easily the hair takes in and loses water; high porosity means a raised or damaged cuticle.
How far a hair stretches and returns without breaking.
The back of the neck, where the hairline ends.
Anything that stops a service or means it must be changed.
Able to pass from one person to another.
The eggs of head lice, glued to the hair close to the scalp.
Ringworm of the scalp: a contagious fungal infection.
A contagious bacterial skin infection with weeping sores and honey-coloured crusts.
A condition in which the scalp makes too much sebum.
Hair loss caused by styles that pull the hair too tightly.
A scale from 0 to 14 showing how acid or alkaline something is; 7 is neutral.
Having a pH close to that of healthy hair and skin (about 4.5 to 5.5).
Having a pH above 7; alkaline products swell the hair and lift the cuticle.
The cleaning ingredient in shampoo; one end is attracted to water and the other to oil.
The foam made when shampoo is worked into wet hair.
Water with a lot of dissolved minerals; shampoo lathers poorly in it.
A strong shampoo that removes product build-up.
A clarifying shampoo that removes minerals from hard water, and chlorine.
Made with milder surfactants than sulphates; gentler on dry and treated hair.
Washing the hair with a cleansing conditioner instead of shampoo.
Oil or conditioner put on before the shampoo to protect the hair.
A conditioner that smooths the cuticle and is rinsed off after a few minutes.
A light conditioner left in the hair after the final rinse.
A treatment that passes into the cortex, usually with heat and a longer time.
A treatment that strengthens weak, over-stretchy hair for a time.
A treatment that puts water and softness back into dry, brittle hair.
Light, smooth stroking used to start and finish a massage and to spread product.
Small, firm circles with the finger pads; the main shampoo movement.
Quick, brisk rubbing with the finger pads to stimulate the scalp.
Slow, firm kneading of the scalp, used during conditioning treatments.
A basin the client leans back into; the most common type.
A basin the client leans forward over; used when she cannot lean back.
Equipment that gives moist heat during a deep treatment.
A plastic cap that holds in warmth and moisture during a treatment.
Where new growth meets relaxed hair; a weak point that breaks easily.
Handling the hair as little as possible to reduce breakage.
A shampoo that rinses out cleanly and leaves nothing behind; used on locs.
Killing most harmful germs on clean tools and surfaces with a chemical.
Killing all germs and their spores.
How long a surface must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.
Sore, red, cracked or itchy skin, often on a stylist's hands from wet work and products.
The client's record of analysis, services, products, timings, advice and any reactions.

c1.title: A plait-up before school in Spanish Town
c1.text: Miss Odessa Reid brings her daughter Brianna, aged 8, to a salon in Spanish Town for a wash and cornrows before school starts on Monday. Brianna keeps scratching the back of her head. As trainee Jhanelle parts the hair, she sees tiny, oval, whitish specks stuck firmly to the hairs close to the scalp at the nape and behind the ears. They do not move when she blows on them, and they will not brush off with her finger. The salon is busy and two other clients are waiting.

c2.title: Dry coils and the steamer in May Pen
c2.text: Kerry-Ann Thompson, 26, comes to a salon in May Pen for a wash and deep treatment. Her shoulder-length natural hair is tightly coiled and has been in two-strand twists for three weeks. It feels hard and dry. When trainee Tameka slides her finger and thumb along a dry strand from the ends towards the scalp, it feels very rough, and water sprayed on the hair soaks in almost at once. A single wet hair snaps after stretching only a little. Tameka plans a deep treatment under the steamer; the maker's leaflet says 20 minutes with steam.

c3.title: Fading colour in Mandeville
c3.text: Mrs. Pearline Campbell, 58, visits a salon in Mandeville for a shampoo and set. Her hair is relaxed; her last touch-up was seven weeks ago, so about 2 cm of tightly curled new growth shows at the roots. Three weeks ago she had a permanent dark brown colour to cover her grey, and it is already fading. At home she washes every few days with a clarifying shampoo and very hot water 'to get it really clean'. Trainee Nordia is doing her service.

c4.title: A wedding rush in Montego Bay
c4.text: It is Saturday morning at a salon in Montego Bay, and five bridesmaids are booked for a wedding. Trainee Rushane is working at the back-wash basins. His first client, Mrs. Shauna Bailey, hurt her neck in a car accident last year and says it still gets stiff. The salon's hot water comes from a solar heater on the roof, and other stylists are using the basins beside him. A hood dryer has been plugged into an extension cord that runs across the floor near the basins, where water has splashed.

c5.title: Clean-up time at the training salon
c5.text: At the end of a practical session in the Centre's training salon in Kingston, the trainees are cleaning up. Ricardo rinses the used combs under the tap and puts them straight into the UV cabinet. Annmarie pours conditioner from a large salon bottle into an empty water bottle with no label, to keep at her station.

c6.title: Locs and braids in Ocho Rios
c6.text: Damion Clarke, 34, a tour guide in Ocho Rios, has worn waist-length locs for ten years. He swims in the sea most days and works beeswax and shea butter into his locs every week. His locs feel heavy and smell musty, and his scalp is oily. His sister Tashana has come with him. Her box braids were put in two weeks ago, her scalp feels sweaty from the heat, and she wants a wash without taking the braids out.

questions.q: What are the specks Jhanelle has found most likely to be?
o: Dandruff flakes caused by a dry, itchy scalp
Dried shampoo or gel left on from the last wash
Head lice eggs (nits) glued to the hairs
Scales from psoriasis that has spread to the scalp
questions.why: Nits are glued to the hair close to the scalp, often at the nape and behind the ears, and will not blow or brush off. Dandruff and product flakes lift away easily, and psoriasis scales sit on the skin, not on the hair.

questions.q: What should Jhanelle do next?
o: Stop, and tell Miss Reid in private what she has seen and where to get help
Shampoo twice with an anti-dandruff shampoo, then plait the hair as booked
Carry on with the plaits, but keep Brianna's comb and towel away from others
Comb out the eggs herself with a fine-tooth comb, then wash and plait
questions.why: Head lice are contagious, so the service must not go ahead. A stylist does not treat infestations: tell the parent kindly and privately, and suggest a pharmacist or doctor.

questions.q: After Brianna and her mother leave, how should Jhanelle deal with the comb, clips and towels she used?
o: Rinse the comb and clips in hot water, and fold the towels for the next client
Wipe the comb and clips with a towel, and hang the used towels in the sun to air
Spray the towels with disinfectant to reuse them, and soak the comb in shampoo
Bag the towels for a hot wash, and clean and then disinfect the comb and clips
questions.why: Lice and eggs can be carried on tools and fabrics. Towels need a hot wash and tools must be cleaned, then disinfected; rinsing, wiping or airing them in the sun does not make them safe.

questions.q: What do Tameka's checks tell her about Kerry-Ann's hair?
o: Low porosity, and poor elasticity from a lack of moisture
High porosity, and poor elasticity from a lack of moisture
High porosity, and poor elasticity from a lack of protein
Low porosity, and good elasticity for very tightly coiled hair
questions.why: A very rough feel and water soaking in at once show a raised cuticle: high porosity. Hair that snaps after little stretch is dry and brittle and needs moisture; hair that over-stretches and feels gummy is the kind that lacks protein.

questions.q: Tameka is running behind with her next client. She wants to turn the steamer up to its highest setting and rinse after 10 minutes. What should she do?
o: Keep to the maker's setting and 20 minutes, and check on Kerry-Ann often
Turn up the heat and rinse after 10 minutes, as more heat does the work faster
Turn up the heat, but put a towel over the cap so the scalp does not burn
Leave out the steamer and rinse after 10 minutes, as heat is only optional
questions.why: The maker's time and heat are set so the product works safely. Extra heat can irritate or burn the scalp and dry the hair, and a shorter time means the treatment may not work; plan the order of clients instead.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann asks how to stop the dryness coming back between salon visits. Which advice suits her best?
o: Use a clarifying shampoo every week to keep the scalp free of oil and product
Use a protein treatment at every wash to make the strands harder and stronger
Co-wash between shampoos, deep condition often, and sleep in a satin bonnet
Wash only once a month, and put grease on the scalp every morning instead
questions.why: Dry, porous coily hair needs moisture put back and kept in: gentle cleansing, regular moisturising treatments and satin at night. Weekly clarifying strips moisture, protein at every wash makes hair hard and brittle, and scalp grease does not moisturise the lengths.

questions.q: What is most likely making Mrs. Campbell's colour fade so quickly?
o: Her relaxer, which goes on breaking down the colour for weeks
Washing too seldom, so oil and dirt build up and dull the colour
Her acid-balanced conditioner, which slowly dissolves the new colour
Her clarifying shampoo and very hot water, which lift the cuticle
questions.why: Clarifying shampoos are strong cleansers, and very hot water lifts the cuticle, so colour washes out faster. Coloured hair needs mild, sulphate-free colour-care products, lukewarm water and a cool final rinse.

questions.q: Why must Nordia take special care when detangling where the new growth meets the relaxed hair?
o: The new growth is more porous than the relaxed hair and soaks up water
The hair is weakest where the two textures meet, and it snaps easily
Relaxer stays active there until the next touch-up and can burn the scalp
The colour is darkest there and will rub off onto the comb and towel
questions.why: The line of demarcation, where curly new growth meets straight relaxed hair, is a weak point that breaks under tension. Detangle from the ends with a wide-tooth comb, holding the hair between that line and the scalp so that combing does not pull on it.

questions.q: Which details belong on Mrs. Campbell's client record after today's visit?
o: Her hair and scalp findings, the products and timings used, and the advice given
The date and the price, as her colour and relaxer details are kept on another card
Only any problems, since a normal shampoo service does not need to be recorded
The products she ought to buy, so the receptionist can sell them at her next visit
questions.why: A full record of the analysis, products, timings, any reactions and the advice given lets the next stylist work safely and shows what was done if there is a complaint. Every service is recorded, not only problems.

questions.q: Before he lowers Mrs. Bailey back to the basin, what is the best thing Rushane can do about her neck?
o: Tilt her head well back so water cannot run forward onto her face
Ask her to hold her head up off the edge of the basin during the shampoo
Offer a front-wash basin or extra neck support, and ask what suits her
Take away the neck rest so that her head can sink lower into the basin
questions.why: A client with a neck problem may not be able to lean back safely. Support and cushion the neck without over-stretching it, or wash her leaning forward; ask her, and stop if she feels dizzy or in pain.

questions.q: During the rinse, the water from Rushane's spray suddenly runs very hot. What should he do first?
o: Keep rinsing quickly, so the hot water stays on her scalp for less time
Ask her whether the heat is bearable before he moves the spray away
Cup his hand over her hairline so the hot water stays off her face
Move the spray away from her head at once, then adjust and retest it
questions.why: Protect the client first: turn the water away from her straight away, then adjust the taps and test on your wrist again. Keeping your fingers in the flow lets you feel a change before she does.

questions.q: What should be done about the hood dryer's extension cord?
o: Tape the cord flat to the floor so that nobody trips over it while it is in use
Switch off with dry hands, dry the floor and move the cord away from water
Put a wet floor sign beside the cord and carry on with the shampoos
Lift the cord onto the edge of the basin so that it is off the wet floor
questions.why: Electricity and water together can give a shock, and a cord across a walkway is a trip hazard. Switch off with dry hands, dry the floor, and keep cables away from basins and walkways.

questions.q: What should Ricardo have done with the used combs?
o: Removed the hair, washed them, then disinfected them for the time on the label
Rinsed them under the tap and dried them well before putting them in the UV cabinet
Wiped them with a damp towel and left them on the trolley for the next session
Left them in the UV cabinet overnight, as a longer time disinfects them fully
questions.why: Tools are cleaned first (hair and product removed, washed), then disinfected for the full contact time on the label, then stored clean and covered. A UV cabinet only keeps clean tools clean; it does not disinfect them.

questions.q: Why is Annmarie's unlabelled bottle of conditioner unsafe?
o: It will not hold enough conditioner to last her a whole session
Conditioner spoils within a day once it is moved to a smaller bottle
Someone could mistake it for drinking water or a different product
Only the manager may open the salon's large bottles of product
questions.why: Products must stay in their own labelled containers. An unlabelled drinks bottle could be swallowed or used wrongly, and the label's directions and warnings are lost.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the musty smell in Damion's locs?
o: His oily scalp is making too much sebum in the heat
His locs stay damp inside after washing or swimming
The sea salt is reacting with the beeswax in his locs
His locs are short of oil, so they are drying out
questions.why: Thick locs can stay wet in the centre for hours. Trapped moisture, along with wax and butter build-up, lets mildew grow and causes a musty smell, so locs must be squeezed and dried right through.

questions.q: Which wash suits Damion's locs best?
o: A residue-free shampoo squeezed through each loc, then dried right through
A rich, creamy shampoo rubbed along each loc, then butter to seal it
A co-wash only, so his locs keep the wax and natural oils that protect them
A dry shampoo powder only, so his locs do not get wet and stay damp inside
questions.why: Locs need a shampoo that rinses out cleanly to remove wax, butter and salt build-up; squeeze it through rather than rubbing, then dry fully. Creamy products and co-washes leave residue trapped inside the locs.

questions.q: How should the stylist shampoo Tashana's box braids?
o: Rub shampoo firmly down the full length of each braid to lift out the dirt
Use firm rotary and friction movements to reach the scalp under the braids
Put diluted shampoo on the scalp along the parts and press it in gently
Shampoo only the braids, as the scalp cannot be cleaned until they come out
questions.why: Diluted shampoo from an applicator bottle reaches the scalp between the braids, and pressing and patting cleans it without frizzing or loosening them. Rinse well and dry fully, as damp braids can smell and itch.

questions.q: Each surfactant molecule in a shampoo has a 'head' and a 'tail'. How do they work together to clean the hair?
o: The head dissolves the oil, and the tail makes the lather that lifts the dirt
The tail soaks into the cortex, and the head smooths the cuticle as it rinses
The tail holds on to oil, and the head to water, so the oil rinses away
The head holds on to oil, and the tail holds on to the hair so it stays clean
questions.why: The oil-loving tails surround oil and dirt, and the water-loving heads keep them in the water so the rinse carries them away. Lather is a side effect; it does not do the cleaning.

questions.q: During a shampoo, which description fits the friction movement?
o: Slow, smooth stroking with the palms to spread the product evenly
Slow, firm kneading that lifts and moves the scalp over the bone
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips to wake up the scalp
Quick, brisk rubbing with the finger pads to stimulate the scalp
questions.why: Friction is quick, brisk rubbing with the finger pads, in short bursts during the shampoo. Smooth stroking is effleurage, slow kneading is petrissage, and tapping (tapotement) is not normally part of a shampoo.

questions.q: Marcia's single hairs are very fine, but they grow so close together that little scalp shows when you part them. She calls her hair 'thick'. How should you record it?
o: Coarse texture and high density
Fine texture and high density
Fine texture and low density
Coarse texture and low density
questions.why: Texture is the thickness of one hair; density is how many hairs grow on an area of scalp. Marcia's hairs are fine, but there are a great many of them, so it is her density that is high.
